final_proof:
Let \(d\) be a positive integer, and give \(\mathbb R^d\) its usual inner product
\[
  \langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^d x_k y_k.
\]
(If \(d=0\) is allowed, the same conclusion holds with the empty orthonormal basis.) First, this inner-product space is complete. Indeed, if \((x^{(n)})\) is Cauchy in the induced Euclidean norm, then, for every \(k\),
\[
 |x^{(n)}_k-x^{(m)}_k|\leq \lVert x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\rVert,
\]
so each coordinate sequence is Cauchy in \(\mathbb R\). Put \(x_k=\lim_n x^{(n)}_k\) and \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N\) such that \(\lVert x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\rVert<\varepsilon/2\) whenever \(m,n\geq N\). For fixed \(n\geq N\), letting \(m\to\infty\) in the finite sum defining the squared norm gives
\[
 \lVert x^{(n)}-x\rVert
 =\lim_{m\to\infty}\lVert x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\rVert
 \leq \varepsilon/2<\varepsilon.
\]
Thus \(x^{(n)}\to x\), so \(\mathbb R^d\) is a Hilbert space.

For \(1\leq i,j\leq d\), the coordinates of the standard vector \(e_i\) are \((e_i)_k=1\) if \(k=i\) and \(0\) otherwise. Consequently
\[
  \langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}.
\]
Hence \(\{e_1,\ldots,e_d\}\) is an orthonormal set.

Now take an arbitrary \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\in\mathbb R^d\). Since \(\langle x,e_i\rangle=x_i\), we have
\[
  x=\sum_{i=1}^d x_i e_i
   =\sum_{i=1}^d\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i.
\]
Thus every vector of \(\mathbb R^d\) belongs to the linear span of the \(e_i\), and therefore
\[
 \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_1,\ldots,e_d\}=\mathbb R^d.
\]
An orthonormal set whose closed linear span is the entire Hilbert space is, by definition, a Hilbert-space basis. It follows that \(\{e_1,\ldots,e_d\}\) is a basis for the Hilbert space \(\mathbb R^d\).
